sections.h: The Son of Man in Enoch's Parables
sections.b:
The Book of Parables (1 Enoch 37–71) is, if it is pre-Christian as most scholars think, the earliest Jewish writing that treats Daniel's "one like a son of man" (Daniel 7:13) as a single heavenly person with a name and a role. He sits beside the "Head of Days" (46:1), was named before the sun and stars were made (48:3), was hidden in God's presence and revealed to the chosen (48:6; 62:7), and will sit "on the throne of his glory" to judge kings, the mighty and the fallen angels (62:5; 69:27–29). He is also called the Chosen One, the Righteous One and the Anointed One (48:10; 52:4). At the very end an angel tells Enoch, "You are the Son of Man who was born for righteousness" (71:14).

4 Ezra 13, from about AD 100, also makes the figure from the sea a single deliverer. Because Matthew alone among the Gospels has the Son of Man sit "on the throne of his glory" (Matthew 19:28; 25:31), the Parables are central to the study of Jesus' title. Most scholars date them before AD 70 and read them as Jewish background to the Gospels; others date them later in the first century (Knibb), to about AD 115–117 (Hindley), or think they are Christian (Milik). Whether Matthew knew them is a separate question. The Ethiopian Orthodox church, which holds 1 Enoch as Scripture, reads this Son of Man as Christ.

common: Most scholars think the Parables were written between about 40 BC and AD 70 and show that some Jews already read Daniel 7:13 as a heavenly judge.
uncommon: Milik (1976) argued that the Parables were a Christian work of about AD 270, which is why they are missing from the Dead Sea Scrolls.
Charles emended 71:14 so that the angel points to someone else ("This is the Son of Man"), keeping Enoch distinct from the judge.

sections.h: Enoch in the Book of Parables
sections.b: In 1 Enoch 37–71 Enoch is the seer who receives three "parables" of the coming judgment. He traces his line back to Adam through Kenan and Jared (37:1), is snatched away by a whirlwind to see the homes of the righteous (39:3), and asks the angels who the Son of Man is (46:2). In the Noah fragments he appears as Noah's grandfather, who answers his cry and explains why the Flood is coming (65:2–12). The book ends with two accounts of his being taken up, which explain Genesis 5:24: his name is raised into the presence of the Son of Man (70:1), and in the heaven of heavens an angel tells him, "You are the Son of Man" (71:14). Later Jewish mystical writing made the taken-up Enoch into the angel Metatron (3 Enoch 3–16).
sections.refs: 1 Enoch 37:1; 1 Enoch 39:3–8; 1 Enoch 65:2–12; 1 Enoch 70:1–4; 1 Enoch 71:1–17; Genesis 5:24; Hebrews 11:5

uncommon: Some scholars read 71:14 as the climax of the whole book: Enoch is the Son of Man he saw, raised up and installed.

sections.b: The Parables call their heavenly judge "his Anointed One" (Ge'ez mäsiḥ) twice: the kings "denied the Lord of Spirits and his Anointed One" (48:10), and the mountains of metal serve "the authority of his Anointed One" (52:4). Both echo Psalm 2:2, where the kings set themselves "against the LORD and his anointed." The Messiah of the Parables is not an earthly king who wins battles, as in Psalms of Solomon 17, but the pre-existent Son of Man who judges from God's throne. This joining of the royal Messiah, Daniel's son of man and Isaiah's chosen servant into one figure is the closest Jewish parallel to the way the New Testament speaks of Jesus.

The Parables are full of the language of choosing. The community calls itself "the righteous and the chosen" (38:2–4; 58:1–3), and its heavenly champion is "the Chosen One" (40:5; 45:3; 49:2; 61:8), a title taken from Isaiah's servant: "my chosen one; my soul is pleased with him" (Isaiah 42:1). The judge and his people share a name. What happens to him happens to them: he is hidden and revealed, and so are they (48:6–7; 62:7–8); he sits on the throne, and they live with him forever (62:14). Luke uses the same title at the transfiguration, "This is my Son, the Chosen One" (Luke 9:35).

sections.h: The fallen angels in the Parables
sections.b: The Parables return to the Watchers story (see 6:1–8:4) several times. Iron chains are forged for "the armies of Azazel," whom Michael, Gabriel, Raphael and Phanuel will throw into a burning furnace (54:3–6); the Chosen One judges Azazel on God's throne (55:4). Chapter 69 gives a new list of leaders and what each taught: Gadreel, who led Eve astray and taught weapons; Penemue, who taught writing with ink and papyrus; Kasdeya, who taught the blows of demons (69:2–12). Michael himself trembles at how harsh their judgment is, yet will not plead for them, "because they act as if they were the Lord" (68:2–5). Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 speak of the same chained angels.
sections.refs: 1 Enoch 54:3–6; 1 Enoch 55:4; 1 Enoch 64:1–2; 1 Enoch 68:2–5; 1 Enoch 69:2–15; Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4

sections.b: In 1 Enoch 40 Enoch sees four faces around the Lord of Spirits and is told their names and work: Michael, merciful and patient; Raphael, over sickness and wounds; Gabriel, over every power; and Phanuel, over repentance and hope (40:9). The list replaces Uriel, one of the four in 9:1, with Phanuel, whose name is drawn from Peniel, "the face of God" (Genesis 32:30). The same four come out of the crystal house with the Head of Days in 71:9 and 71:13. The Parables also name "those who never sleep," the cherubim, seraphim and ophanim (61:10; 71:7), and angels of the winds, thunder, hail and dew (60:12–22).
sections.refs: 1 Enoch 40:1–10; 1 Enoch 60:12–22; 1 Enoch 61:10; 1 Enoch 71:7–13; Daniel 10:13; Luke 1:19; Tobit 12:15

sections.b: The Book of Parables has its own name for God, used more than a hundred times and almost nowhere else: "the Lord of Spirits" (ʾƎgziʾa Mänafəst). It seems to be a reworking of "the LORD of Armies" (YHWH Tsevaot), the name the seraphim sing in Isaiah 6:3, and the Parables' own version of that song reads, "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Spirits. He fills the earth with spirits" (39:12). God is also "the Head of Days" (46:1; 71:10), from Daniel's "Ancient of Days," and "the Lord of kings" in the kings' confession (63:2–4). Hebrews 12:9 calls God "the Father of spirits."
sections.refs: 1 Enoch 39:12; 1 Enoch 46:1; 1 Enoch 63:2–4; 1 Enoch 71:10; Isaiah 6:3; Daniel 7:9; Hebrews 12:9; Numbers 16:22

sections.b: Several passages in the Parables speak in Noah's voice, not Enoch's: chapter 60 (dated "in the five hundredth year," Noah's age in Genesis 5:32, and with Enoch called "my grandfather"), 54:7–55:2, and 65:1–69:25. Noah sees the earth tilt and cries out to Enoch, who explains why the Flood is coming and promises that Noah will be kept (65:1–12). God tells Noah that angels are building the ark (67:1–2), and Noah receives Enoch's "book of the parables" (68:1). Most scholars think these come from a lost "Book of Noah," also echoed in 106–107, in Jubilees 10:13 and 21:10 and in the Genesis Apocryphon from Qumran.

common: Most scholars think a lost Book of Noah lies behind 1 Enoch 60 and 65–69.

sections.b: A Noah fragment says that on one day two monsters were separated: Leviathan, a female, sent to the depths of the sea, and Behemoth, a male, sent to a hidden desert named Dendayn east of the garden (60:7–9). An angel adds that they are kept for the day of judgment and "will feed," so that God's punishment is not in vain (60:24). The pairing goes back to Job 40–41 and Psalm 74:14. 4 Ezra 6:49–52 and 2 Baruch 29:4 also tell of the two monsters made on the fifth day and kept as food for the righteous at the end, a theme the Talmud develops (Bava Batra 74b–75a).

sections.h: Behemoth and the desert of Dendayn
sections.b: In 1 Enoch 60:8 Behemoth is male, Leviathan female, and Behemoth "with his chest holds a desert that no one can see, named Dendayn," east of the garden where Enoch was taken up. The name Dendayn is uncertain: some connect it with the land of Nod east of Eden (Genesis 4:16), others with the eastern desert. Here, as in Job 40:15–24, Behemoth is God's creature, kept for his purpose.

1 Enoch 51 is one of the clearest promises of resurrection before the New Testament: "In those days the earth will give back what was entrusted to it. Sheol will give back what it has received" (51:1). The Chosen One will choose the righteous from among the risen dead and sit on his throne (51:2–3). In 61:5 even those lost in the desert, eaten by fish or by wild animals "will come back," and in 62:15 the righteous "will have risen from the earth" and "put on the clothing of life." Compare Isaiah 26:19, Daniel 12:2, John 5:28–29 and Revelation 20:13.
sections.refs: 1 Enoch 51:1–5; 1 Enoch 61:5; 1 Enoch 62:15–16; Isaiah 26:19; Daniel 12:2; Revelation 20:13

sections.b: When the Head of Days takes his seat in 1 Enoch 47:3, "The books of the living were opened in front of him." The prayer of the righteous has been heard, and "the number of the righteous" is complete (47:4). The scene joins Daniel's court, where "the books were opened" (Daniel 7:10), to the book of those who will live (Daniel 12:1), and it is very close to Revelation 6:9–11 and 20:12.

A short poem in 1 Enoch 42 tells of Wisdom, who went out to live among people and found no home, so she went back to heaven and sat among the angels. Wrongdoing went out instead and found a home, "like rain in the desert." The poem reverses Sirach 24, where Wisdom settles in Israel, and is close to Baruch 3:9–4:4 and to John 1:10–11. In the Parables wisdom returns with the Chosen One, in whom "the spirit of wisdom" lives (49:3), and it is poured out "like water" at the end (49:1).
sections.refs: 1 Enoch 42:1–3; 1 Enoch 48:1; 1 Enoch 49:1–3; Sirach 24:1–12; Baruch 3:9–4:4; John 1:10–11; Proverbs 8:22–31

sections.b: In 1 Enoch 47 the blood and prayers of the righteous rise to the Lord of Spirits. The angels join their prayer that justice would be done "and that they may not have to wait forever," and the holy ones rejoice when "the number of the righteous" is complete (47:1–4). The scene is very close to the souls under the altar in Revelation 6:9–11, told to wait until the number of their fellow servants is complete, and to 4 Ezra 4:35–37.

sections.h: The kings and those who hold the land
sections.b: The enemies of the Parables are not idol worshipers in general but "the kings, the mighty" and "those who hold the land" (38:4; 62:1–3; 63:1). They trust in their wealth and their scepter, persecute the faithful and deny the Lord of Spirits (46:7–8; 63:7). On the last day they will see the Son of Man on the throne of his glory, beg for mercy, confess that God is "the Lord of kings," and find it too late (62:9–12; 63:1–12). Many scholars see in them the Herodian rulers and great landowners of first-century BC Judea.

The Book of Parables calls its three main sections "parables" (Ge'ez məsale, 37:5; 45:1; 57:3; 58:1; 69:29). They are not stories like Jesus' parables. The word follows the Hebrew mashal, used of Balaam's oracles (Numbers 23:7), which covers riddles, proverbs, poems and visionary speeches. Each of Enoch's parables is a revelation about the coming judgment, the Chosen One and the fate of the righteous and the sinners.
sections.refs: 1 Enoch 37:5; 1 Enoch 45:1; 1 Enoch 58:1; 1 Enoch 69:29; Numbers 23:7; Ezekiel 17:2

sections.h: The righteous dead pray for the living
sections.b: In 1 Enoch 39:5 Enoch sees the homes of the righteous with the angels, "They were asking, pleading and praying for the children of humans." In 47:2 the holy ones in heaven join the prayer of the righteous on earth. The passages are among the early Jewish texts used in later debates about whether the saints pray for the living (compare 2 Maccabees 15:12–14 and Revelation 5:8).

sections.h: The burning valley and the hot springs
sections.b: In 1 Enoch 67 the angels who taught wrongdoing are locked in a burning valley in the west. Hot waters flow from it, smelling of sulfur, and the kings use them for healing; one day they will turn to fire that burns forever (67:4–13). Many scholars connect the waters with the hot springs of Callirrhoe by the Dead Sea, where Herod the Great sought treatment shortly before his death (Josephus, Jewish War 1.657). Compare the lake of fire in Revelation 20:10 and the "eternal fire made ready for the devil and his angels" in Matthew 25:41.
